title: New Year's Post
caption:
This year we saw the world change at a rapid pace - physical landmarks gone, icons of our culture lost and more and more influence of all things artificial. 
And yet, we held on tight to what is genuine and human. This year we will be mindful of keeping to our core principals of authenticity. 
But we can't do it alone. Jetty is based on connectivity. It's up to all of us in this greater community to continue to lift up what is real. 
Here's to living the truth in the New Year.
notes:
23 years deep. Still growing. Still giving back. Still pulling ink, chasing swells, and standing behind the people and waters that shaped us. None of it happens alone, and all of it happens with intention. As we head into 2026, we’re more grateful—and more fired up—than ever.

title: Piper's Story
caption:
Help Us Send Piper Abroad! ✈️🌍❄️
The 11th Annual Arctic Outreach is almost here! Join us at our NEW location, Hollow Pines, on March 7th from 11 AM – 5 PM for a day of fun.
Arctic Outreach began to raise funds for Mallory McBrien in her time of need. Arctic is hosted in memory of Mallory each year and continues to support her family and so many more thanks to your support.
This year all funds from the 50/50 raffle will benefit Piper McBrien (Mallory's daughter), as she looks to join the American Music Abroad program this summer! We’re helping this amazing Southern Regional student raise the funds needed to join the American Music Abroad tour this summer.
Find those 50/50 tickets and help support a local student!

Read Piper’s story in her own words:
"Hey, my name is Piper McBrien and I live in Manahawkin NJ, with my dad Tim and brother Cedar. I have been a part of the Arctic Outreach since the beginning. This event is held every year and presented by The Jetty Rock Foundation, in Memory of my mom. The proceeds from the event help support our community and those facing hardship. For the past few years I have been a volunteer at the event as I understand how important it is to give back to our community. The community continues to support my family. Currently I am a student at Southern Regional High School and a member of the Strings Orchestra. I have been playing the violin for almost 6 years. This year I have the opportunity to participate in the American Music Abroad for high school students in July, perform at different venues, and tour 5 countries. I am so excited to see the world, learn about different cultures, and make new friends, all while getting to play my violin. I can't express how excited I am, and I believe the memories I make will make this one of my best summers ever."

title: Global Recycling Day
caption:
It’s Global Recycling Day! 
As some of you might know, we’re big fans of Shell Recycling and the incredible impact it has on our local ecosystems.

But why do we do it? Here’s the "shell" of the story:

- Used shells provide the perfect foundation for new oyster growth and restoring reefs.
- A single adult oyster can filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, creating clean water.
- Instead of sending these beauties to a landfill, we return them to the water where they belong to help build strong and healthy marine habitats.

Jetty Rock works tirelessly with organizations such as @soilconservationdistrict to support the COASTAL project, the @lbtfieldstation supporting their Clam Cove restoration project and the use of recycled shell from our partnering local restaurants, as well as working and supporting @nj.dep and @newjerseyfishandwildlife Shell Recycling program.

All these collective efforts ensure that the next time you’re enjoying some oysters or clams, those very shells become the building blocks for a more resilient coastline, thriving marine life, and a cleaner ocean for generations to come.

title: National Oyster Month: Week 1
caption:
Starting National Oyster Month off by reviewing the species you might encounter at your favorite restaurant. 

Did you know that every oyster you eat, grown from Maine down to the Gulf of Mexico, is the exact same species? While they taste different based on where they're grown (that’s the "merroir"!), they are all Crassostrea Virginica (The Eastern Oyster).

Across the rest of North America, there are 5 species widely grown you're likely to see on raw bar menus:
Eastern (Our local hero!)
Pacific
Kumamoto
Olympia
European Flat

No matter the name on the menu, if it's grown on the East Coast, it’s likely a Virginica!

title: National Oyster Month: Week 2
caption:
For week two of National Oyster Month we are highlighting how oysters are the hardest working shellfish in the bay. A single adult oyster can filter up to 50 gallons of water in just 24 hours.
As bivalves (mollusks with two shells), they act as natural water purifiers, removing excess nutrients and keeping our coastal ecosystems crystal clear. This is why Jetty Rock Foundation is so committed to putting recycled shell back in the water! More shell means more habitat for more oysters, more oysters mean cleaner waters for all of us.

title: National Oyster Month: Week 3
caption:
No Brain? No problem! 
It's true... oysters do not have a brain. BUT don't let that fool you. They are survival experts and while they can’t swim away from predators (they are "sessile," meaning they stay put once they land), they have a heart, stomach, and kidneys.
They also pack a punch for your health! Oysters have the highest naturally occurring levels of Zinc, an essential mineral for your immune system. 
Who needs a brain when you’re a nutrient-dense, water-cleaning powerhouse?

title: National Oyster Month: Week 4 Post 2
caption:
Ending National Oyster Month with a chat about spat! 
Have you heard of the term "spat" or "spat on shell"? That's the official name for a baby oyster! Once these tiny larvae are ready to stop swimming, they ideally find a hard surface (another oyster shell preferred) to attach themselves for life and begin growing. 

By keeping your shells out of the trash through various shell recycling programs and partners, you are providing the base baby oysters need to build the reefs of tomorrow. Through our partnership with the @soilconservationdistrict and local farmers like @laughinggulloysters, we are able to plant spat-on-shell onto restoration reefs as part of the ongoing COASTAL Grant Project.

Happy National Oyster month! Lets keep protecting our coast, one shell at a time!

title: Coquina Surfer Highlight: Christine Best
caption:
We’re kicking off our Surfer Highlights with a long-time competitor and friend: Christine Best.

Christine has been navigating her cancer journey since 2021. After facing an advanced progression in her bones earlier this year, she’s successfully reversed course, is walking the beach pain-free, and plans to be back on her board by January! While she isn't surfing in the event this year, she'll be helping out hands-on right from the sand.

"Having cancer is all about the pivot and seeing the small things that you lose appreciation for. I am just so grateful to walk out on the beach and watch people living their best life." 

This is Why Your Support Matters:
Coquina Jam proudly partners with David’s Dream & Believe Cancer Foundation (alongside Jetty Life & the Jetty Rock Foundation). 100% of the proceeds raised at the event go directly to local cancer patients to help cover day-to-day living expenses and costly treatments.

title: DEP Shell Planting Recap
caption:
Last week, the crew and @reclamthebay joined @nj.dep @newjerseyfishandwildlife on the Mullica River for a morning of shell planting as part of the State's Shell Recycling Program! 🌅🦪
As part of the program, oyster and clam shell from area restaurants, cured for a bit on land, and then placed in the Mullica River. We lent a hand hosing off the barge to plant 1,200 bushels of shell that will become habitat for soon spawning oysters in the river. New clean shell will allow spat to and grow and add to local oyster populations. Huge thanks to our partners at NJDEP Fish & Wildlife for allowing us to join them for a morning of fun and helping us make an impact!

title: Spat Count Recap
caption:
Did you think we'd keep the boat clean for long? This week we lent a hand and a ride to the Ocean County Soil District and Barnegat Oyster Collective farmer Matt Gregg to head out on the water and collect samples for the COASTAL Project. Pulling samples from their spat on shell and bringing them on board, our crew assisted in counting each and every tiny oyster on the recycled shell (spat on shell). With counts and some additional measurements, everything was placed back into the water to continue growing.

You can support the COASTAL Project and other oyster initiatives by grabbing your ticket to the Raising Shell Oyster Social on 8/26. Head to the link in our bio for more info.

title: Enviro post
caption:
From shell to shore, small actions can make a big impact. 
This summer, we’re highlighting the people, programs, and projects working to protect the waters we call home. From recycling oyster shells and returning them to the bay to supporting oyster growers and reef restoration, there’s a lot happening beneath the surface.
Swipe through for a few local environmental updates, and learn how you can get involved. 

Jerm (BLOG):
We didn't know much about oysters in 2016 when recent Golden Otis award winners Corinne Ruff & Angela Andresen came to us with the idea to create a documentary. The Oyster Farmers premiered shortly after that in January of 2018, but before we even finished the film we realized that our call to action was to repopulate our local waters with oysters. In short, East Coast oyster reefs are only ~1% of what they were in the mid-1800's (Read more here). We were quickly educated on what became a new hero to us, crassostrea virginica, or the eastern oyster. Oysters filter water, create habitat, protect shorelines, and support an industry that you might not be super familiar with. The farmers in New Jersey's waters were sparse, especially after Hurricane Sandy, but many have started businesses since and are as resilient as the oysters that they farm.
The Winter of 2025/2026 was a frozen one, literally. Prolonged freezing, thick bay ice, wind, and extreme low tides didn't make it easy on the farmers, nor their gear. You probably didn't think about that when you were slurping down oysters this Summer though. Many farmers lost significant money trying to track down scattered gear and oysters. Oyster mortality, increased labor costs, and reduced inventory likely led to a multi-year financial hole to dig out of for many. Cold water isn't necessarily bad for oyster production as it can reduce the spreading of diseases like Dermo and MSX, but last Winter was one of the coldest we've seen in years.
We've been supporting oyster growers and the industry overall since our Jetty Rock Foundation (JRF) supported the educational documentary. First, we partnered with Dale Parsons and Long Beach Township to create the first-ever municipal-run oyster recycling program in New Jersey. Soon after, the State of New Jersey sat with us and initiated the Atlantic City Shell Recycling Program which is run through NJ Fish & Wildlife. We've financially supported both programs although they have took it largely upon themselves to fulfill the mission of collecting shells from local restaurants, cure the shell, then return it to the water. Farmers step in and assist to complete the cycle with restoration efforts. 
Now some 10 years later, JRF's oyster initiatives live within our Raising Shell program whose goal is to "elevate oysters, their growers, and the industries and communities connected to them"
Today we partner with the COASTAL RCCP Project the JRF has pushed helping to fund (9) local oyster farmers pursuing spat on shell restoration on their leases. We accelerated that support by hosting our inaugural Raising Shell Oyster Social last month. We've also worked with and supported the NJDEP's Project S.H.E.L.L initiative which provides environmental trips for NJ school students and revamped Stafford Schools' class trips by funding eco-trips for all grades (K through 6th). Partnering with Minorities In Aquaculture and Oyster Master Guild has helped spread awareness well beyond Jersey. Since 2017, we've contributed $445,825.14 to oyster farmers, partner organizations, and initiatives. We accelerated that support by hosting our inaugural Raising Shell Oyster Social last month. This was all about oyster education, but beneath that we paid the farmers above-market price for the oysters that they supplied. From clean water to economic implications, we're committed to doing everything that we can to support the oyster industry...and now we have a brand new boat (thanks to Tito's), so we can get out on the water for research, education, and restora

title: Clam Jam 20 years
caption:
Slide 1: 
For 20 years, the Clam Jam has brought our community together to celebrate great waves, forge lifelong friendships, and honor the memory of our dear friend, Patrick Harrington. As we wait for the perfect swells to arrive for this year's event, we’re looking back through some favorite years. Dive into the full story and read favorite memories shared by friends.

2007:
"My favorite Clam Jam will always be the first year, when Brendan and Conor Willem won. It was such a monumental moment for me. These were two kids I watched grow up on the same block, winning the inaugural event put on by some of my closest childhood friends. Their father, Bill competed as well. To see Jetty create their own surf contest, them win that first one, and then see what Clam Jam and Jetty have grown into over the past 20 years makes that day pretty special. It was one of those moments where our little LBI surf community, friendships, and history all came together." @whereisrandal

2008:
"2008 was my favorite because it was so new and so raw. Matty G was my partner. That day was a raging nor’easter. We built a hut on the beach the night before to block the wind. I paddled out six blocks to the north because of the drift and got a bomb right away. Unfortunately, the heat hadn’t started. I wore a full set on the head and that ripped my jersey off. Had to run back up and paddle out again. But what a day." @snorkel_boy

2012:
"2012 was the first year back at Hudson after the first round of beach replenishment on the island. The contest had a brief stint on the south end while the sand got sorted out, but Hudson has always been an epicenter of surf for the local community and it turned on in proper fashion that day. The weather was about as good as it gets for mid October and we had perfect a-frames thanks to Hurricane Rafael way out in the Atlantic. Just an all around 10/10 day and not a thought in the world about what was to come. That community on the beach rallied in a big way in the following months and its hard to separate the time leading up to Sandy from the aftermath."  @kgronophoto

2020:
"Twenty years of the Clam Jam! Congratulations!
We have so many memories of the Clam Jam - it seems like each year we had the chance to meet someone new, see old friends, cheer on the newest groms on the LBI Surf Circuit and enjoy the place we love to call home. Knowing that Patrick’s name is on the trophy as a finalist always brings a smile to our faces; it was a cold day - late in the season - but we knew leaving until his day was over was out of the question. While that is a fun day to remember, our favorite memory -  though bittersweet - was the Clam Jam of 2020. It ended up being Patrick’s final Clam Jam. It was obvious that day Patrick was pretty sick and that treatments had worn him down. We feel, however, Clam Jam 2020 embodies everything the Jetty Clam Jam represents. Patrick was able to get down to the beach and spent his time sitting on the beach talking to friends, fellow surfers and past partners. So many came by and sat and spent time with him. He was still a part of the surf community here on the island, even though he hadn’t been in the water for 15 months.  It was so good for him to be able to catch up with everyone there - many of whom he hadn’t seen in a while. It reinforced to us just how loyal and deep this community of surfers is - and how much they truly care for one another. We think it was the perfect example of the brilliance behind the idea of the Clam Jam. We are grateful for the memory of that day and look back on all the Clam Jams with love and fondness.” - Denise and Jim Harrington

title: Enviro Post: The "R" Season
caption:
🦪 The “R” months are here and that means it’s prime oyster season! 🍂
Ever heard of the “R Rule”? Legend says you should only eat wild oysters in months containing the letter R.

Why? Back in the day, before refrigeration, warmer non R months (May through August) meant higher spoilage risks. Spawning also typically occurs during these warmer months, which not only made oysters thin and watery, but would remove them from the water prior to them creating many, many more oysters. Once autumn hits and the temperatures drop, oysters plump up, store energy, and hit peak flavor!

At JRF, we’re big oyster fans!
1. Because they’re delicious.
2. Because they have great impacts on coastal ecosystems, filtering water and creating habitat.

When you enjoy local oysters at participating restaurants, those shells don't go to waste. Through local Shell Recycling Programs, we return them to the water to restore living shorelines, improve water quality, and create habitat for local marine life.

Tell us! How do you like your oysters and where’s your go to spot? 👇

caption:
We're stoked to showcase the 20th Annual Clam Jam Merch! Be sure to grab your commemorative tee and hat at the event! 

REMINDER:
This weekend is Chowder Cook-off which the Jetty Crew is heavily involved in, so there will not be a Clam Jam on October 3rd or 4th. We will continue to wait for a proper day with the next potential dates being October 10th or 11th.

If you’re registered to compete, keep a close eye on your texts and emails for direct updates, and for everyone else, turn on post notifications so you don’t miss the green light.

Registration for the 2026 Jam is still OPEN but spots are limited and you must be invited to register.
